title: Maitreyi's question
hookLine: Nani says the line by heart, and why the tradition puts hearing first
carry: shruti: the holy word is heard first
tomorrow: after the card, Nani has one note for Priya. what is it?

lines: A CARD, A LINE OF THE GITA.
cards: A grandmother opens a birthday card and finds a line from the Gita written inside, in careful, slightly wobbly Devanagari. She glances at it and doesn't read it.
She says it, the whole verse, by heart, eyes on her granddaughter instead of the page. She learned it the way she learned her first songs: by ear, long before she read it.
Which raises today's question: why does this tradition put hearing first?

teach.b: Start with a name. Hindus call the Vedas shruti, what is heard: tradition says seers heard them, and teachers handed them on mouth to ear, keeping every sound. And there's a story about what that hearing is for.
In the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, the sage Yajnavalkya is about to leave home for the life of a renunciant, and offers to divide what he owns between his two wives.
One of them, Maitreyi, asks him: if this whole earth, full of wealth, were mine, would it make me immortal? No, he says. Your life would be like any rich person's life.
Then what would I do with it, she says. Tell me what you know. So he does.
The Self, he tells her, is what should be seen; and the way there is hearing, then reflecting, then meditating. Hearing comes first. Now a neighbor that also begins with the ear.

In Judaism, a line from Deuteronomy is said morning and evening, the Shema: "Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one." Shared: two old traditions that open with listening, not looking. And an honest difference.

teach.h: ONE KEEPS THE LETTER, ONE THE SOUND.
teach.b: The Shema declares the one God, and the Torah is read from a scroll written by hand, every letter kept. The Vedas, tradition says, were carried by voice, every sound kept.
Both are ways of listening closely enough that a holy word isn't lost.

how: Vedic chant is traditionally taught by a teacher reciting and students repeating, phrase by phrase; many Hindu families also teach children prayers and Gita verses by ear before they can read them.

o: Sanskrit's sounds, learned by ear before the eye
Sanskrit's sounds, learned only from printed books
Sanskrit's sounds, kept secret from new readers

p: turns down wealth to ask what lasts

s: Judaism and Hinduism keep their holy words in exactly the same way
one keeps every letter on a handwritten scroll; one kept every sound by voice.
Maitreyi asked whether all the wealth on earth would make her immortal
Yajnavalkya said no, so she asked for what he knew.

games.q: a friend from a Jewish family says her grandfather taught her the Shema by ear, before she could read Hebrew. what's a fair thing to say?
o: that's shared: both traditions start with hearing, though they keep the words differently.
that's the same as the Vedas; it's one practice with two names.
that's different: Hindus learn only from books.
games.why: shared: listening first. honestly different: the Shema declares the one God from a handwritten scroll; the Vedas were carried by voice.

practice: With eyes open or closed, listen to the farthest sound you can hear, then the nearest, then your own breath. Don't name them; just hear them, the way a student hears a teacher's line before saying it back.
When the mind starts talking, go back to listening.

wordCard.voice: The sounds: in a tradition that calls the Vedas shruti, what is heard, the ear comes before the eye.

orig.note: Sanskrit: what is heard; the name for the Vedas.

carryVoice: Hold on to it: shruti, the holy word is heard first, and the reading follows after. See you tomorrow.
